utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With respect to the audiotape, Mr. President, we would appreciate the opportunity to make a written response to the written submission made by the Prosecution. We'll have that available within a day or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. You can have seven days normally to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Would you please tell the Court your name.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Milenko Arapovic. I was born in Busovaca on the 16th of November, 1969.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Arapovic, you signed, on May the 8th, 2000, a one-and-a-half-page affidavit. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This was signed in front of a judge in Vitez, Judge Maric; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you check the statements made in the affidavit carefully to ensure that they were accurate before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. What I signed is the truth, and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You stand by the statements made in that affidavit today, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So far as this witness is concerned, there are matters that I want to ask him that mostly are effectively matters of credit, but also arguably extend beyond that and beyond the content of his affidavit and relate to matters that have been touched on directly in evidence, not least by Witness T.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think the point has come, Your Honour, when it's time to make objections to extensive cross-examination that goes way beyond the scope of direct examination or the factual statements made in the affidavit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll hear the argument. What is the relevance of this? I don't remember Witness T.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So perhaps you could remind us what the point is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness T dealt with an incident at Tisovac in the spring of 1992, and since I don't understand the evidence given by Witness T to have been accepted or admitted on behalf of the defendants, it would be quite absurd for the Chamber not to take the opportunity of checking with this witness whether what has been said about him is accurate or not. I'm going to say after the adjournment something more about the use that's being made of affidavits and the effect it's having on the trial, but it is, in our respectful submission, unrealistically confining when you have a witness who is actually spoken of in a trial directly and where it's suggested that the Prosecution can't ask questions relating to direct and material evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question, Mr. Nice, is whether when an affidavit is tendered and the Chamber rules that the affiant be brought for cross-examination, does he become a witness at large, or is he still not a witness in respect of the evidence in the affidavit?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I would respectfully suggest that the last proposition would be absurdly limiting and entirely artificial. The Chamber makes the decision as to which witnesses it wishes to hear. Indeed, I thought when the Chamber was referring to this witness that the Chamber had already become aware of the fact that his name had been mentioned earlier. It may be the Chamber wasn't having in mind Witness T's evidence, it had in mind some other part of the evidence about the checkpoint incident. So I may have misunderstood the Chamber there. But in answer to Your Honour's point, once the witness is here, it would be artificial, in the extreme, to say that he's not a witness at large, in my respectful submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, if you continue to the adjournment, I shall remind myself of what Witness T said during the adjournment and we'll consider the matter afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Arapovic, tell us a little bit about the preparation of your evidence. Had you been seen at an earlier stage by lawyers or anybody else acting for the defendant Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: The contact was established, I think, about two years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that with lawyers for Kordic or with lawyers for anyone else?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where did you see them?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: I think in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At that time did you have any documents to show them; did they have any documents to show you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I mean, as a citizen of the municipality of Busovaca at that time, I naturally watched media so I knew that Mr. Mitko was Mr. Kordic's lawyer, and there was no need for me to try to learn anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You misunderstand me. I don't mean documents for Mr. Mitko to show who he was, I mean documents about the incident in respect of which you were going to give evidence. Did you have any documents to show them, the lawyers; did the lawyers have any documents to show you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What incident do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you gave your affidavit, what was the evidence you were giving all about? Tell us.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was the locality called Kacuni where the BH army stopped at the checkpoint, without announcing it previously, Mr. Kostroman, and all the rest. If need be, I shall repeat it all as it was. So we were coming back, I think, from Travnik or Stari Travnik, from a session --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pause for a minute. I'm going to ask you about that later. When the lawyers first saw you a couple of years ago, did they see you about that incident or did they see you about something else?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: Only about that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They didn't ask you, for example, about anything that may have happened at a place called Tisovac; just yes or no to that.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did they show you any documents, any contemporaneous documents or otherwise, when they spoke to you about the checkpoint incident a couple of years ago?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: We only talked about it, and I naturally stated what happened that day and how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. When you then saw them more recently for the preparation of your affidavit, when was that? When did you see them in relation to the preparation of your affidavit?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, the judge in Vitez merely summoned me to read my statement. I read it and I saw that it was all true, as I said it before, and I signed that statement in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The statement that you say was presented to you before the judge, when was that statement actually drafted?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: That statement was drafted when I saw Mr. Mitko for the first time, which was two years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you sign the statement at that stage?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you arrived at the judge's for your affidavit, the statement was already in final form, was it, just waiting for you to sign it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: I read the statement once again, studied it and saw that nothing had been changed from what I said two years ago, that it was all as correct as it was then, and then I naturally signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Without any alterations.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: Needless to say, without any alterations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us, then, please, how you remember this incident. Do you have your own diary?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have any diary about that. But if you have 50 rifles pointing at you, then you don't forget that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just before we move forward, had you had any contact with the lawyers in that intervening two-year period?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So what was the date of the incident, please?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, don't ask me about the date. I remember the month. We were coming from Novi Travnik or Travnik, from a meeting, and I was in Mr. Kordic's car --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there. Don't ask you about the date; you can't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: You know, there were so many dates, Your Honours, I really can't remember every one of these dates. Every day has a date. I know it was the month of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, you see, if it be the case that your affidavit has a date in it, that can't have come from your memory presumably because you don't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, there were two instances when we went through Kacuni. January was when we were attacked by the BH army, and it was then when I stayed in the area. I cannot remember the exact date, that is, when the checkpoint was put up. I simply know that we were coming back from Novi Travnik or Travnik, passing through Busovaca, where we left Mr. Kordic at home after we heard over the Motorola that the BH army had set up a checkpoint at Kacuni. Mr. Kostroman, who parted company with us in Kacuni, he wanted to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've read all that. We don't need to go through it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that a convenient moment? We'll adjourn now. Mr. Arapovic, could you remember during the adjournment not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and not to let anybody speak to you about it. That does include members of the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we've had the opportunity of looking at the evidence of T, which was about a specific matter in relation to this witness. That we consider you can put. It's clearly relevant, if for no other reason than it goes to credibility. More generally, as far as the cross-examination of these witnesses is concerned, we think it should be limited to matters in the affidavit or to matters going to credibility, unless there is some specific point, as this one is, which would allow wider cross-examination. What we do not think is that it should be the opportunity for a roving commission, because to do so would, to some extent, defeat the whole purpose of having affidavits, which is to try and achieve an expeditious trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Arapovic, have you in the break taken the opportunity to read your affidavit again?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: On that day in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. Today.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: So that was now, in May?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Today, in the last half an hour, have you taken an opportunity to read --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. I want to go back to what you've been saying about seeing the lawyers two years ago and making a statement two years ago. That statement -- or let's get to what you mean by two years ago. Can you be a little more precise? We're now in the year 2000, so two years ago takes us back to, at the very latest, some part of 1998. Yes, 1998. Can you tell us when it was that you saw the lawyers, please?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: That must have been the summer or fall. I could not recall. Somewhere around the middle part of the year, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, you made a statement to them. At the time that you made the statement, what detail of the allegation or of the evidence did they have? What did they tell you was the evidence that had to be dealt with?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: You see, it referred to that day, the date when we went from Novi Travnik and Travnik to Busovaca, and Mr. Kostroman, in the direction of Kresevo, that is, the road that takes you on to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you informed that the Prosecution were going to lead evidence about what the Prosecution said happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: You see, I just had to explain what happened that day. We never discussed the Prosecution. I don't know why we should have discussed the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, you see, your statement that's been prepared, or your affidavit that was prepared in that two-year period -- I don't mean -- at some point in that two-year period, deals with one incident and one incident alone. It deals with Mr. Kostroman, the car, and his release at the checkpoint, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how you did this. You reduced it. My statement is much more detailed. I can repeat all the details. From Novi Travnik and Travnik, and then what was -- what we heard in Busovaca, and then what happened at the checkpoint, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. What your affidavit does is deal with that. It deals with coming from Travnik to Busovaca through Vitez, it deals with what happened then and what happened to Mr. Kostroman, but it deals with this single incident. And what I want to know from you, please, is: When you were asked about this at some time in 1998, did the lawyers have with them some summary or did they present to you some summary of the evidence that the Prosecution was going to lead on this topic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not recall all the details, but what I put down in my statement is how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that statement that you made two years ago, have you had a chance to look at it since then and to compare it with the affidavit that you made at the Court?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, Your Honours, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But you would be happy for -- would you be happy for other people to see that earlier statement, if it exists, in this Court?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I said what I said at that time and then I signed it. I don't know what other statement you're referring to. It's the same statement as it was then, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, I'm going to suggest to you that what you tell us can't be accurate, because the detail of what passed, according to the Prosecution witnesses, at the checkpoint was simply not served on Defence lawyers in 1998, and therefore there can have been no way, unless I'm mistaken -- if I'm mistaken, I'm only too happy to be corrected -- there can be no way they can have got you to deal with these matters in detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you answer that or not? It seems to me more of a comment, really. Mr. Nice, perhaps you'd move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've made my position clear, and I want to know this:

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say in your affidavit, reflecting your earlier statement, something about how Mr. Kostroman was released. How was he released?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: I think that had we not made it to Kacuni, where Mr. Kostroman had been stopped with his escort, that it would have been an end for him, because when you have 50 to 100 barrels pointed at you, you put yourself in that position and decide for yourself. Had we not arrived and parked right next to him -- he was already being pointed toward the silo, which was near the main road. So we talked to them, we negotiated with them. Mr. Bogdan knew one of the Muslims from Busovaca, and he said, "You can pass, but Mr. Kostroman stays." And then we said, "If he stays, we are staying. It's either/or." You should have been in my place or in Mr. Kostroman's place in order to know what was going on. And the UNPROFOR who arrived -- actually, UNHCR, for us they were -- to us they were all the same. This was all in the beginning. We didn't distinguish between them. Had they not arrived, I think that we all would have ended like Mr. Petrovic and other men who died at that checkpoint. So, Your Honours, that's all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What I want to know is: In your first statement two years ago, did you mention UNPROFOR or UNHCR as being instrumental in some way in releasing Mr. Kostroman?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think the UNPROFOR or UNHCR, I think arrived by pure accident. Had they not arrived, we would have been buried under ground now, like the ones before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you mention UNPROFOR and UNHCR when you spoke to the lawyers sometime in 1998? That's all I want to know. If you did, it will be in your statement. And if it's there and I'm shown it, I shall be happy to accept it. Did you mention UNPROFOR or UNHCR when you saw your lawyers -- not your lawyers; Mr. Kordic's lawyers -- in 1998? I don't want to take any bad points in this case, you see.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have already stated. What I said in the statement, that was so. If I had not mentioned UNHCR, that means that nobody had prepared me for this, because one cannot recall everything. But now I am sure that the International Community representatives arrived, and they in a way couldn't pass through, because these obstacles were erected at the checkpoint by the ABiH, the ones that are called hedgehogs, or apex obstacles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And just finally, before I move on, this must be right, musn't it: There must have been a reference to UNHCR or UNPROFOR in your original statement, because when your affidavit was presented for you for signing at the Court on the 8th of May of this year, it didn't require any amendment, alteration or additions; you just signed it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: I first read it through, and I came to the conclusion that it was the way it had been written down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. You, I think, were a member of Mr. Kordic's special bodyguards; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: I was his personal security. I don't know where the word "special" comes from, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it right that you were regularly in that work in company with Damir Cosic and Bogdan Santic? Are these regular bodyguards?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As bodyguards, you had special training; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: You see, who could have had any special training at that time? I was what I was. Apparently I was good enough, so I remained in that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How were you selected?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: On the 26th of April of 1992, when the JNA bombed the town, I happened to be there by accident, and when the bombs started falling we started running. You may appreciate how it looks when you're being bombed and you're there with a pistol in your holster. I happened to be by Mr. Kordic, and as the buildings were burning and several people were also killed, I was with Mr. Kordic that night, by sheer accident, and then it just continued from there, because somebody had to be with that -- with this man.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's right, is it not, that at some stage you had been to both Grude and to Zagreb in the course of the war. Was that for training purposes?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: During the war I never left Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us about this: The Tisovac -- one other question. The group to which you were a member, were they called the Scorpions?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I never heard of the unit called Scorpions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you give any explanation for how that name might be associated with you? Was there any name of a group that might be similar to "Scorpio" or "Scorpions"?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: I already said, I don't know of a Scorpio unit or anything like it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the time that you say you were recruited you had a pistol. In what capacity was it that you had a pistol at your belt?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. What kind of recruitment are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, you told us how you had a pistol, how Kordic was there, houses were burning, and you continued because somebody had to look after him. That's what I'm referring to. How come you had a pistol with you at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: You see, big things were going on in Croatia. The Croatian people were suffering and being killed there, and we supported them back home by taking over some barracks; that was one way of helping out our suffering brethren in Croatia. Obviously, in those barracks there were all kinds of weapons, long-barrelled and short-barrelled, and many other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the spring of 1992, you were already guarding Mr. Kordic up in Tisovac. Do you remember an incident when a couple of men, probably going fishing, were stopped by you and arrested and taken to the Tisovac area?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that day the gentlemen that the Prosecutor is referring to were invited to stop at the checkpoint in Tisovac but they didn't stop. The home guards which were manning the checkpoint were unable to do anything. Then they called us on the field telephone, that those gentlemen did not obey their orders. I don't know how quickly they were able to fish but they were already past us up there, and so I quickly went with some guys. We saw them walking by the river; they were even skulking about. We called them and we said, "Weren't you told to come back?" This was downstream from the Ivancica River. We told them, and I quote, "Gentlemen, you have to go back to Busovaca. This is not a place for fishing. We have our offices here." They then obeyed, they complied, and they walked away. I think that we even secured a vehicle for them to go back to the town. That was all that happened on that day, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before they were allowed to return to the town, you took them and forced them to strip, didn't you? Why was that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I didn't do that, nor any of my fellow soldiers who were there with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was only when Grubesic took over that they were released; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I hear this for the first time now, and I say that it is not true. Before I sat down in this box, I read my statement and I was told that I would be asked only questions from this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've presumably been told that something may be asked of you about your being named as a war criminal, have you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: From which side? By whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you been named as a war criminal?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: I hear this for the first time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By the court in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. But when Zenica could do it, it would condemn all the Croats of Central Bosnia, right off.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you accept, then, that you may have been named as a war criminal in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I object to that question on the grounds that it calls for speculation. The man's been asked the question does he know and he says he doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I could show him the documents but I don't want to take time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Go on to the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to suggest that you are and probably know that you've been named as a war criminal in Zenica for ethnic cleansing and other offences; isn't that the truth?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: Those allegations are not true, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a couple of more questions, then. The meeting you were coming from, what was it all about? That is, on the day of the Kostroman event, what was the meeting you were coming from all about?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the negotiations were conducted between the Croatian and Muslim side, but I wouldn't know what was discussed because I wasn't present there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Or is the reality that you were actually at a meeting in Fojnica, travelling in the reverse direction from that which you have described?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: That is absolutely not correct. We were going from Travnik or Novi Travnik. I said that I have given an oath or a declaration here, and based on that I say that we went from Travnik or Novi Travnik. I don't know where this idea came from that we were coming from Fojnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You, as Kordic's bodyguard, know perfectly well that he was present and that, indeed, he made a threat in the course of the disarming of a man at that checkpoint on that day. That's the truth of the matter, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: I already stated that those allegations are not true. Mr. Kordic stayed at home, and after what we heard via the Motorola about the checkpoint which had been erected between Silo and Kacuni, we went there in our vehicles. I already said what would have happened had we not arrived and had the UNPROFOR not -- that is, the UNHCR not arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, the UNHCR or the UNPROFOR were in a position to log, to record, this incident if they'd wanted to, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the gentlemen's duties were at the time. I don't know whether they were supposed to assist both ethnic groups to protect us, and I don't know what they were supposed to log.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I should have said, I am obviously -- but would be grateful for sight of the witness' earlier statement, if that is made available, in particular in relation to the point that I'm making about UNPROFOR and UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Arapovic, two years ago when you were speaking with Mr. Naumovski, he didn't have you to sign a statement, did he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a leading question. The damage has been done. Did you sign the statement that Mr. Naumovski showed you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO ARAPOVIC
utterances.text: You mean in 1998? I can't remember, I really don't know if I signed it or not, but I know that we discussed it and that I stand by what I said at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's the only question that I had, Your Honour, but if the Court wants to hear from Mr. Naumovski, as far as we are aware, there is no such signed statement. The witness was never asked to sign one and did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Arapovic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll turn next to the question of the affidavits. Before we do that, it may be convenient to deal with one other matter. Mr. Nice, you asked us yesterday to delay consideration of the motion on adjudicated facts. Are we to take that as, in effect, a withdrawal of the motion which you proposed to resubmit at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not so much withdrawal as amend down, yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a very equivocal answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It has to be the same motion because it's the same application, but what I would forecast is that in due course the Prosecution would seek to rely on limited, probably far more limited findings than those necessarily listed on a broad basis at the time of the making of the original application; and that the degree to which we can reduce the original application will be best known at the end of the evidence by which time the progress of the other appeals will be better known as well. Now, obviously the ideal position, in one sense, for tidiness would be for us to amend down to nothing, for us to say that we don't seek to rely on anything. I think it's unlikely that we will go that far, but I think it highly likely that we will amend substantially so that only a limited number of matters will sought to be relied upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that your answer remains ambiguous because you present us with a motion and you say that the contents of which will be examined at a later stage, which means it remains open. So you have to decide when you present such a motion to the Trial Chamber, you do it for the Trial Chamber to give an answer. If you think that it is not on the agenda any more, you should withdraw it and then present another motion, an amended one, and then you should tell us so at a point which you deem to be appropriate. But you can't leave open a motion in front of the Chamber without determining the actual status of this motion. We would have preferred had you given us more clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry that it seems or is unclear. The technical reason for my proceeding in this way was to forecast before the end of our case and remains -- the technical basis for proceeding this way, and let me try to explain it again. If one looks at all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Don't really try to prolong this debate. I have understood all too well the reasons. But this is thus a matter of procedure. It is simply a technical point. You speak about a motion. I ask you not to give an answer to this motion and say that it will be presented at an appropriate moment. It would have been better to withdraw it and then present the motion at another time. My point is merely a point of procedure. It's nothing about the contents or the substance about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I quite understand that. The point I was trying to emphasise was that there had to be within our Prosecution case and before the end of the Prosecution's evidence an application to rely on judicial facts elsewhere, because assuming, one way or another, this case reaches the Appeals Chamber, there may be technical issues raised about what was the state of the evidence at the end of the Prosecution's case. And it was with that possibility in mind that it seemed appropriate to raise the issue by the general application that we made before the end of the Prosecution's case, and for that reason it seems to me still possibly safer to proceed by way of later amendment. But it, in substance, would be little different from, if different at all from, withdrawing this one and making a further more limited one at a later stage. But I would ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Nice. We shall treat it as if it's withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Then the arguments on both sides that exist in these pleadings can probably be incorporated for economy at later applications when made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I turn next to the affidavits. At the conclusion of this discussion, there is a further matter I want to raise and it concerns the progress of the case. We are in the position where we must start listing other cases before this Chamber, and therefore we need the assistance of the parties about the future of this case. So after this matter we will have some discussion on that. The affidavits have come before us, complete with a summary of affidavits 13 to 20. It may be convenient to deal with them. We've also had an application to admit a portion of a transcript. It may be convenient to discuss that too. But we'll begin with the summary of the affidavits. Number 13 is Jozo Sekic. We've ruled on that. The next one is Mr. Branko Golub, affidavit 14, from Fojnica. Is there any point the Prosecution want to make about him?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I deal with --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Golub, can I make some general observations about affidavits, and inform the Chamber that our slight concern about the present circumstance is something we're going to reflect in a written motion in a day or so. In short, we are going to be expressing concern on a number of affidavits that are coming in, and inviting the Chamber to exercise caution before admitting them in this volume. The position at the moment is that some 25 affidavits already, I think, have been served, to be contrasted with the position in the Prosecution's case where a total of 12 were intimated. Of those, five were ruled out, simply on the grounds of lateness, despite their having been forecast and subject to the possibility of reviving them in rebuttal, and despite the fact that they covered the same territory in form as the material dealt with in Your Honour's absence on the other side a couple of days ago. So there's those five. The other seven, I think it is, one falls into a special category, because it was Mr. Morsink, and he was provided at the direction of the Chamber. And the others were notified in November, in the overview of witnesses, and in due course dealt with at the end of the case. Now, so numerically there's a very stark contrast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, pausing there, one needs to look at the history of the matter. I don't know when it was that there was first an intimation that you might call affidavit evidence, but as I recollect, there was difficulty which you experienced obtaining them. And also this has got to be looked at against the background of a developing practice in a new institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All of that I accept, and indeed for Your Honours's assistance, I think the utility of the affidavit rule was mentioned first to me probably informally even before the case began, so its potential interest in Chambers of this institution is well-known -- interest to. I accept that. And Your Honour is quite right; we had very grave difficulties, including opposition by the Defence, as to the legality of what we were doing, in our way. Nevertheless, there was only a limited number that we sought to call, and although, of course, sometimes on contentious issues, not on absolutely central issues. And the Chamber will recall that our general approach to non-direct evidence was that matters that should be admitted should have gone in in some other way, and so on. Now, the present position is that there is a small flood of affidavits, outnumbering, I think -- is it outnumbering it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Not outnumbering the live witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In fact, I think the number is 21, and there have been 30 live witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, but beginning to match it. And these, which of course deprive the Prosecution of any cross-examination, are affidavits on central issues, such as Mr. Kordic's role, presence, and so on. So that there is a stark difference in our two approaches. We have in mind the continuing stance of the Kordic defence in the Appeals Chamber, where they maintain that the simple objection by either party to the adduction of an affidavit is determinative as to whether the affidavit can be called, which is why I have announced and continue to express an objection in principle to all the affidavits, save those which I expressly say are agreed; none so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we've got the general drift of these submissions for general submissions, and you're going to make them in writing and then we'll consider them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm mentioning it now so as not to be thought that I'm changing my position. What we're inviting you to do is to have the overall landscape in mind. Because, for example, if the Appeals Chamber rules in favour of the interpretation of the Defence, and the Defence now prayed in aid in their latest pleading, in observation of Your Honours last week, to support their position. If they rule in favour of that interpretation, then there will be no affidavits on either side, and that is something that we've got to have in mind, or we would invite you to have in mind, when you consider the balance between affidavit witnesses and others. But yes, indeed, our position in writing will be coming your way in a day or so's time. We've prepared a short schedule of the Defence affidavits that I think are going to have to be dealt with today. Can I hand that in? Meanwhile, can I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you accept any of these affidavits?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I maintain my objection to all of them. As Your Honour will remember, the approach I was taking was to identify, having made my in principle objection, I was then to identify special reasons relating to individual ones, or particular reasons, as I spoke of earlier, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And as to this witness, the first one, Branko Golub, you'll see that we have analysed the points of evidence in the affidavit and the points which it is said it can act as corroboration, and therefore here there's a reasonable match. And I don't think, subject to what I observed at an earlier stage, I think, about paragraph 12's generality, I don't think there's anything particular beyond the general that I refer to on this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can admit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll admit this. The next one is Dr. Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We have made a separate filing in respect of that which sets out our position. It seemed particular --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me find that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: To remind ourselves, this is the doctor --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- seeking to produce documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- which then say something about the mental health of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He was at the Busovaca Medical Centre, known the witness for some time, saying he's reviewed various documents pertaining to Mr. Cicak's disability --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- and confirms they are authentic, including a letter of discharge from his work. And your objection --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are many objections here, apart from the fact that the witness wasn't asked about any of this. And I don't actually have the pleading myself, but don't worry about that. I can remember it; at least, I can remember most of it. The problems include, so far as the utility of Rule 94 is concerned, that the witness in whose support he is said to be, or one of them, if Your Honour recalls, had no knowledge of mental ill health, and eventually reduced his evidence to: He had a feeling about him, or something to that effect, and it got worse, because it was then revealed that the only reason he put anything in his summary about mental ill health was because he had been told by the lawyers that the doctor had found the man to be mentally unwell or mentally ill. Completely circular, and therefore what Dr. Pavlovic would be corroborating was his own material, because his material then found its way into the witness's summary. The witness says that's what the doctors say he is, and they then sought to bring the doctor in to corroborate. So wholly unsatisfactory on technical grounds. But in any event it's expert evidence, and not served as expert evidence. In any event, it's hearsay. And on top of all that, there are serious questions of privacy which are sourced in the motion, but I don't have it before me at the moment, which would make it inequitable and wrong for this evidence to be given. And I refer again to the fact that the witness himself wasn't asked about these matters and hasn't had a chance to deal with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You refer, so we can have it in mind, in your submission to the jurisprudence of the European human rights organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The European Commission says the collection of medical data and the mentions of medical records falls within the sphere of private life, Chare, nee Jullien, against France. And you refer to a textbook of -- an English textbook on the subject, and also the legislation from various countries, such as Germany, repressing, as it's put, unauthorised access to and disclosure of personal data contained in private or public databases. There is also the broad objection, with which those of us from common law systems will be familiar, about the attacks on the credibility or otherwise of witnesses; the mounting, as it were, of discrete and different issues outside the central issues in the case. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, indeed. I was going to express that in a less well-articulated form by saying that of course there's no evidence connecting whatever his mental state may have been with any unreliability in his evidence. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just a number of responses. I'm not going to respond generally to the attack on affidavits unless the Court wants a general exposition. I think the Court knows what the arguments are. We've had a very long trial. We must find a way to expedite it. We think we've found a way to expedite it by introducing affidavits on insignificant, collateral matters that are corroborative of the testimony of a live witness. You're going to hear from a live witness, one witness after this, about the particular issue that this affidavit corroborates. I want to emphasise that this is not a private medical record. This is an administrative proceeding which was conducted in order to evaluate this gentleman's continued ability to work. And insofar as the insinuations made by the Prosecution to the effect that no cross-examination on this subject was concerned, I merely have this to point out, page 1533 and 1534 of the transcript, where I asked the gentleman, "You were retired at the time, were you not?" And he says, "I was never retired." I asked him, "Were you ever treated by Dr. Petar Pavlovic. He says, "I think you've got the name wrong. He's a very good man. Mr. Pero Pavlovic never treated me." And then there was a direct question from Judge Robinson to the witness, "Did you retire or did you not?" I don't have that before me right now. We'll try to get it in the seconds available. But I have a very clear recollection of that question, and this gentleman gave a very good emulation of Rudolf Nureyev for trying to dance around the question and never answering it. But we have the answer. He was retired in 1984, and it was as a result of a proceeding conducted by the Zenica branch of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina's Institute for Evaluation of Work Ability. I think that Dr. Pavlovic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, Mr. Sayers, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- Dr. Pavlovic sat on the panel which considered this matter. He simply authenticates the documents from the Zenica institute, saying, "Yes, this is an accurate copy of the finding, assessment, and opinion. Yes, this is an accurate copy of the discharge letter," and the documents basically speak for themselves. If the Court wants us to bring along Dr. Pavlovic to say exactly what is stated in the affidavit, we will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The issue is one of admissibility; it's not whether we want the doctor here for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The issue, really, is whether this evidence is admissible or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's precisely the case, Your Honour. We had to evaluate what is the value of bringing the doctor here to say what we could get him to say in an affidavit, to authenticate documents that speak for themselves, that are not controvertible. These are not private records. The person whose eligibility for early retirement was considered had an opportunity, as I understand it, under the law of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to file an appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Sayers. In order for us to be able to follow what you're saying, the problem which you are speaking of is to know how much does this affidavit follow the framework of Rule 94, which means can it corroborate a statement made in front of this Chamber? At first glance it doesn't seem so; it doesn't seem that it corroborates any other witness' declaration in front of this Chamber. Could you please explain, when you mention the document, the document which says that this person has actually retired, if I managed to follow you well, has this document already been tendered, or are you going to do so? Is there an official document? I think, if I understood you well, there is such an official document. Will this witness come here in order to confirm it? Could you give me more clarification, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. First of all, in addressing the privacy matter, I want to emphasise that this doctor was not the personal physician of Mr. Cicak. He was simply a member of a fitness-for-work review board, and as such a determination was made that Mr. Cicak was not eligible to work and that's why he took early retirement. As you see from the documents that are attached to Dr. Pavlovic's affidavit, and we say this -- I think he authenticates the finding, assessment, and opinion of April the 14th, 1984, Exhibit A, as being an accurate copy of an official document --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, will you slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- and the same thing with a letter of discharge, dated April the 14th, 1984, which is authenticated as being an accurate copy of that document, paragraphs 11 and 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, we are agreed on one thing: that it's not appropriate to have this witness as an affidavit witness. If he is to be called at all, he must be called live. Speaking for myself, I have doubts about admissibility, as I've indicated, and I could put them to you for your consideration when you're considering whether to call this witness. First of all, the issue of privacy, which is certainly arguable; secondly, the issue of whether he's an expert or not; he's authenticated these documents as a doctor and therefore prima facie sounds like an expert; thirdly, the question of relevance, whether it's really going to take this case any further to hear that one particular witness retired early due to mental illness. Perhaps you might like to consider all those things when you're deciding what to do next. But we'll not admit it as an affidavit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. If we have to bring the doctor along, we'll do that. As I say, I don't think that his direct examination will last very long at all. Who knows how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You better consider whether he's an expert and the way to approach that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We'll consider that too, obviously, and comply with the appropriate provisions of Rule 94 bis, if that's way the Court wants us to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Also you have to consider the issue of privacy which has been raised, but there's no need to argue that. The affidavit is not admitted. Let's move on to the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next one is Jure Carava, and this is subject to very specific objections. This affidavit doesn't fall within the provisions at all and in any event should be excluded when one looks at what's sought to be done. It's said to be supportive of Niko Grubesic. The points of evidence are, if we deal with them in each case, summarising what the witness would say and what it would be supporting, if anything: He's a member of the command of the Zrinjski Brigade. The witness only mentions Dusko Grubesic as being commander for most of 1992 and 1993. Over the page, it's suggested that he can give evidence that Kordic never had military authority over that brigade which was under the command of Blaskic. The only evidence given there of that is that the witness doesn't believe he had a headquarters at the PTT building. Although the Zrinjski Brigade had headquarters there, he didn't know whether Kordic was there or not, as he wasn't there. So there's no support or corroboration there. Three, Grubesic never took orders from Kordic in relation to the humanitarian convoy on the 28th of April. In cross-examination the witness said he didn't know who was in political command over Grubesic. His view is that the chain of command went via Blaskic. Basically he's ignorant of this matter and isn't suggesting that the incident didn't happen at all, just that he didn't know about it. Four, Dusko Grubesic never orchestrated the seizure of a 40-truck convoy on the 28th of April, no such convoy was taken, and to that he only says he's never heard of such a convoy, that is, the witness. There was a leading question about it in any event. What is being sought in reality with this affidavit is to get in by a door, maybe a back door or a side door, evidence, really, about the commander of Dusko Grubesic, who maybe isn't going to be called. He's listed. His evidence doesn't corroborate the evidence given by the witness, who himself is not in a position to say many of the things that it's sought to have corroborated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is Dusko Grubesic on the list?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He's on the list. He's on the list, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, you're going to call Dusko Grubesic?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We have not made a final decision with respect to him, we reserve our right to do so, but I don't know whether it's going to be necessary to do so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Maybe it's sensible to consider the application of this affidavit after Dusko is called or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I entirely agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If it's corroborative of him. It also goes to, I must say, looking at it, an important issue in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, yes. That as well, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, we have in mind waiting on whether Dusko Grubesic is called and then considering this affidavit. These are important issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let me just respond, if I may. First of all, I think it's rather unfair to put us in the position of producing something like this in open court, this document that the Prosecution has given us, and ask us to react on our feet. But I will react on our feet. Firstly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If it was unfair, Mr. Sayers, I wouldn't allow it. It's not unfair. You know your case. These are perfectly fair points. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This is not submitted in corroboration of the testimony of Dusko Grubesic, and our summary says exactly that. It's submitted in corroboration of the testimony of Niko Grubesic. Second, Jure Cavara was in the staff headquarters of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade until he took over command of that brigade from Dusko Grubesic in the autumn of 1993. This affidavit is submitted in corroboration of the points that we've summarised on page 4 of the document that we've submitted to the Court, including Mr. Grubesic's testimony that there was no seizure of any UNHCR convoy on April the 28th, 1993. So this affidavit stands or falls by itself. It is submitted in corroboration of the specific testimony of Niko Grubesic, to whom we asked specific questions about these subjects. Once again, if the Court wants to bring him here simply to say what he said in his affidavit, I'm sure we can arrange that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not a question of simply saying what he says in his affidavit. The question is whether he should be cross-examined about these matters, whether it's unjust to the Prosecution to allow the affidavit evidence to be given without any cross-examination. That's the issue. But if you want us to make a decision about this witness, we will at this stage, but it may be better to leave it and decide here whether Dusko Grubesic is coming, in which case we can deal with it then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think we should make the decision at this point, Your Honour, because that may have an input into our overall witness selection for the remainder of our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We shall not allow this affidavit. This is clearly an important issue, a number of important issues in relation to the chain of command, and the witness should be called. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ivo Brnada is a name which will be familiar to the Chamber, because his name appears as one of the cosignatories on that arguably important document, Z100, countersigned by Kordic as HVO vice-president, and although that's not the only time that he appears with that title -- indeed we've seen a video clip with him being introduced by that title -- it's plainly a title being rejected on his behalf, or said to be of no significance. Thus far no one has been able to explain the signature, and we see -- it's over the page in Brnada -- that all that the witness Niko Grubesic could say about it was that he'd heard about the order which he hadn't seen before and didn't know whether that position existed. It's interesting to note in the summary of the next witness to be called but one, the mayor of the municipality, that he was present at the meeting but claims to have left before the document was drawn up and therefore would himself be in no position to explain how the signatures were appended and why that particular job title was chosen. So -- and I take you to this straight away, although it's not the only point on Brnada's evidence -- if this evidence is allowed in by way of affidavit, it may be we will have no opportunity of discovering from somebody who must know, assuming that Kordic doesn't give evidence himself, we may have no opportunity of discovering from someone who must know why that document was countersigned by the defendant in the way he did. For that reason alone, it's vital to have that witness before you as a witness to be cross-examined. Going to the earlier four points, number 1, it's not material. Number 2, the agreement as to the 50/50 share allegedly reneged on by the Muslims, the evidence that witness gave is to the effect, summarised, that he doesn't know about the agreement. He sets out something about Draga going to the Croats, Kacuni to the Muslims, and the Croats to get the Kaonik barracks, with weapons equally divided, but I'm not sure that he went further than that. As to 3, the contingent of Muslims, headed by Merdan, arriving on the 9th of May, it may be that on review of the evidence the witness and counsel calling him were in some state of confusion over Kaonik and Draga barracks; Merdan was not mentioned at all and the Kaonik barracks were taken over by the Zrinjski barracks on the 10th of May, the witness unaware of whether Kordic was involved. We would say finally in relation to number 4 that the evidence is unclear. So that as to corroboration, effectively of no value, because it's not clear that it's corroborating matters that are given by the witness. But in any event this signature on Z100 is not a trivial matter; it's an important matter, and it shouldn't be avoided by the witness or not made available to us by the witness not being called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before we hear from Mr. Sayers, I just want to say that in my view in considering these matters, the centrality of the issue is perhaps more important than the corroborative significance of the effect of the evidence, and I think argument should be more directed to that, to show that the issue that the evidence addresses is so central that the person should be called for cross-examination. Also, in my view, corroboration in that Rule cannot be anything more than purport to corroborate. I think that is all it means. So that eventually it will be for the Chamber to assess the question of the weight of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm grateful for that assistance, with the way Your Honour is approaching the problem. And in relation to this witness, as I hope I've made plain, the issues, particularly of the barracks, and in particular Z100, the document that deals with, it may be thought, the takeover, are absolutely central issues and issues upon which the Chamber would require assistance as to how it came about. That Kordic signed, and signed in the capacity he did, is really a central issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, insofar as the document Z100 is concerned, there isn't any dispute from the Defence's part that the signatures are on there. They're in there in the capacities stated. There is, I think, equally no dispute in the evidence thus far that as of this extremely early date in the evolution of the HVO, which is an organisation that was about a month old at that time, there was no office of vice-president. In fact, the office of vice-president was not created, as we know from looking at the paper trail, until the -- until about the 17th of -- 14th of August, when the first vice-president, Mr. Ivanovic, was appointed, and then there were two other vice-presidents appointed in October. The Court has already heard evidence about that. The publication in the Narodni List testified by about Dr. Ribicic established that beyond doubt. So the centrality of the issue, I don't see it being a central issue. The signature is the signature, the described title is the described title, and the Court knows what the circumstances were under which that document was signed. But once again, if the Court wants Mr. Brnada to come to Court and be exposed to cross-examination to test whether what he said is true or not, we're more than happy to bring him along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sayers, I would like to ask a question. Maybe you could assist the Chamber, in order to try to have a fair and expeditious trial. You say that on the one hand the signature is not important; on the other hand, it is important, we don't dispute anything, and the rest is not as important. Why do you really introduce this affidavit? What is the new thing that it brings -- this is the matter, in fact -- if apparently the Prosecutor attaches a certain importance to the question of the signature, the signature which is here, and in the way in which the signature has been interpreted? We can read that Dario Kordic was never an HVO vice-president, although the title appears in document Z100 because the Croats did not have any formal organisation and so on and so forth. And you say: We don't contest anything, we don't dispute anything, we don't dispute the signature. Could you explain to us what is the interest of this particular affidavit?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, happily, Your Honour. The affidavit simply corroborates the testimony of Mr. Grubesic, and Mr. Grubesic was completely unaware of Mr. Kordic being a vice-president, or indeed that there was any office of vice-president as of this time. It should be emphasised once again that this is the very earliest embryonic time in the evolution, not only of the HVO on a national level, but certainly on a local level. In fact, I believe it's uncontroverted that there was no HVO prior to the date that document was actually signed, which was on the evening of May 9th or May 10th. So that's the -- it's not that the affidavit brings anything new. It doesn't. That's not the purpose of an affidavit. The purpose of an affidavit is to corroborate that which is in evidence, and that's what we think it did. The only importance that we attach to the signatures -- I don't think that it is an important issue, and I've explained why. We do not contest the accuracy of the signatures. They speak for themselves. And furthermore, the putative capacities in which the persons who signed the document sign it are explained on the document. The Court has had plenty of evidence about the circumstances under which this document was signed. It knows what the circumstances are. It can make up its own mind whether, in fact, Mr. Kordic was an HVO vice-president within a month of the formation of the body from the signature of the decree by Mate Boban and there being no prior to documentation to this effect in Busovaca. But once again, as I stress, if the Court feels that it's important, in fairness to the Prosecution, I guess, to have the signatory of this document come and explain those facts and be subjected to cross-examination on that, we're happy to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask you, then, Mr. Nice this time: Do you dispute that for you the signature was actually made in his capacity as vice-president, I mean the signature of Mr. Kordic? Is this the disputed point? Is this where you would like to cross-examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The central issue here is what was going on at the time that Merdan was being arrested and agreements were being withdrawn and so on. Was Mr. Kordic a military man with military authority? Was he the supreme authority in the area? As to his technical position, we're probably unaware of whether he was in any sense technically the vice-president. What is important is that he signed this document in this capacity and that he was the authority signing the document, and the only people who can explain that fully are those present at the moment of signing and the two signatories. But as to the suggestion that it matters not whether he was HVO vice-president or not, the Chamber will recall that when I led a little bit of videotape where he was introduced as the vice-president, the cross-examination was clearly aimed at minimising the significance of that by saying, "Well, he didn't say he was vice-president. He was simply introduced as vice-president and he never acknowledged it." So whatever is now said, there is concern in the Defence camp about this adoption of an apparent high rank. We say the adoption, whether reflecting underlying formalities or not, of that rank, is important and reflects the real authority of the man at the time, as the signatories to the document would be able to reveal. So in answer to Your Honours's question, it's not really technically the title and so on; it's the overall circumstances in which he signed using that title.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. He must be called for cross-examination. We'll continue our consideration of these affidavits after the adjournment, and then we'll hear some further evidence when we've also considered some dates. An hour and a half. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.08 p.m. 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Bohutinski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next three, no special observations to make. The Chamber can see the degree and relation to which the third, Zarko Zec, is not in fact corroborative. But notwithstanding that, bearing in mind the concerns of the Chamber, no special observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will admit all three. There's another one come in, Mr. Bilanovic. Have you had that, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we have, I certainly haven't considered it, I don't think. I think there were four others, is it, that have come in recently but I don't think they're due for consideration this week. The ones that we've just dealt with are those that were due for consideration somewhere in the seven-day period ending about now, I think, and although this may offend technically the seven-day rule, it may be thought that the convenient way is to batch whatever is outstanding now until the end of the week and to deal with those at some convenient point next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, all of the outstanding affidavits corroborate the testimony of Mr. Maric, which is expected to be over by this Friday, so one week from then would be the appropriate point within which to consider them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That, then, concludes the matter of the affidavits. I wanted to consider the question of timing. The Trial Chamber has got to list other cases, not just this one. Mr. Sayers, you can help us with this. It appears that we are running on schedule to date. I know you're going to point out that three more witnesses are going to be required as a result of this morning's rulings, but I note that in the 24 days of the Defence case, 30 witnesses have been heard, or will have been heard by tomorrow or the day after. I think you told us that that was about half the case. Is that as I recollect?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. That was based upon our then estimates, and I haven't had the opportunity to consider the position in light of the Court's rulings today. But let me just assure the Trial Chamber that we are going to do our level best to keep our word and to try to have this case put in by the August break, and currently, notwithstanding the addition of three witnesses at least, we anticipate that that will be feasible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The position is that there are some 30 to 35 days left before the break, so you have not as yet had half the time. Do you anticipate that it's possible you might finish before the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Prior to today I would have said yes because I have to admit that our trial strategy was to bring to court those witnesses that we thought were necessary and not to waste the Court's time with those witnesses that we did not think were necessary. I'm sure the Court can appreciate that the rulings today have ramifications beyond the three immediate witnesses. So I'm not as sure as I was this morning that we would be through earlier than the break. That's a possibility but I really cannot say for certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will work on the assumption for the moment that your original estimate is the right one, and that is that you'll finish by the recess.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We certainly have not been dragging our heels, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We will work on that basis. Mr. Kovacic, assuming that that is right and that you will start your case on the 4th of September, I think you told us that two months was the time estimate which you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I did. I'm trying also to submit, and I will do that as soon as I find some time, new details. I'm sure that that is the maximum amount of time that I will need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Of course, there is no need, probably, to remind you about the variable elements which, unfortunately, does not allow me to give you some more precise estimate. But I'm pretty sure that within that time I can do it, one way or another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. If necessary, you may be called on to start your case before the recess, although at the moment that is not on the cards. But it's still a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to be prepared, and in the case that the Kordic Defence will be done earlier, I will be prepared to deliver at least 10 to 12 days of the case before August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. But at the moment it looks as though September the 4th is the date, and we'll work on the basis that you will be finished by the end of October, which would be something like the 27th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps it's a good time just to mention one thing -- I'm not proposing anything -- but I would just like, indeed, to share a problem which I feel could probably arise during the next couple of weeks. I don't know whether the Court is informed, and I'm sure that my colleagues from the other desk will add something --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This may be something we ought to, in the general interest, deal with in private session, if it's the topic that Mr. Kovacic and I were discussing just before, for reasons that I'll come to in a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If Mr. Nice thinks private, it could be private. I didn't want to go into the details, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll go into private session, and then we can hear what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And perhaps if I can help with what our thoughts are in case they are helpful. Obviously if the Kordic case finishes before the recess, very desirable for the Cerkez case to start immediately, because if you look to the end of the time period, Christmas and next year are looming up. Even if one eliminates, or truncates to a minimum, any gaps between cases, defence and rebuttal, there is likely to be a period of time that has to pass between the close of the evidence and submission of written arguments, although there's no doubt those can be prepared substantially in advance. I assume that it will be mutual exchange of written briefs, followed by the usual comparatively short period of time for oral argument in court. And being realistic, I would hope that we can all work towards those stages being completed before Christmas. But unless we keep our feet on the accelerator, in the way we are all doing, there's a terrible risk, one can see, of the thing extending into another year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What I can tell you we have in mind at the moment is to start another case at the beginning of November, that being the close of the case for Mr. Cerkez, and before rebuttal evidence, to allow a short period for rebuttal and rejoinder evidence. You would then no doubt ask for a short period before having to have the briefs in. But the whole matter to be concluded, as far as evidence and submissions are concerned, by the end of the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I'm pretty sure, without having discussed it with my friends opposite, that everyone would share that sentiment. I don't see anybody nodding, but then I don't see anybody shaking their heads either. And we will, of course, do everything we can to ensure that that happens. May I very respectfully invite the Chamber to consider making that a priority concern even over the listing of the other case, because the consequences of this case going after Christmas, where it could go before, are pretty unappealing, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This case has the same priority as any other case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, quite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have to have those cases in mind. At the moment that is what we propose to do, in very general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And I would be grateful if everyone would have that sort of timetable in mind, and if anything is likely to affect it, to let the Trial Chamber know as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour was going to deal with the affidavit of Ljuba Vidovic, and in particular the transcript. This has been, I hope, sufficiently set out in our short application. In our respectful submissions, it would be entirely fair that that passage of her transcript should be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers, is there any objection?.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In conformity with the previous position taken in the case, if a piece of Ms. Vidovic's testimony is to be considered for admission, we would prefer all of her testimony to be considered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We think there's force in the submission that the whole transcript should go in. The whole transcript goes in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: May I add something. I think in general taking one sentence outside the context is not very honest in the sense of the methodology of analysing texts in general. I say it is not compatible with certificate analysis of whatever text it is. Taking the sentence outside of the context doesn't signify anything in general. So if you take the whole text and then you say, "We are relying on this part or this one," then it's different, but just taking a sentence doesn't mean anything. Of course, I am speaking -- this is my personal view, on my own. I am not speaking on behalf of the Trial Chamber in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's helpful to know what Your Honour's views on these matters are. In this particular case we had, of course, put in a couple of pages because they thought that was context enough. But with the whole statement or the whole transcript in, then the overall context will be available. It's the same pages upon which I think we will be relying, but I'm grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have the next witness. Mr. Sayers, we'll go on until ten past four. I take it this will be Mr. Bilic?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would you please state your full name for the Court.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: My name is Zoran Bilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
