utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, I'm going to go over very quickly with you some basic details concerning yourself. It's true, I believe, that you were born on January the 4th, 1951, in the village of Granice, which itself is in the municipality of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You are a Serb by ethnicity and a practising Orthodox Christian.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You're a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you live in a small village or hamlet near Kaonik that contains five other Serb houses apart from your own.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You're married and you have four children, all of whom still live with your wife and you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe, sir, that by training you are a locksmith and that you worked in Zenica for 22 years for a metal parts manufacturer called Metalno.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You worked there until April of 1993, when the Muslims who controlled the company fired all non-Muslim employees; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was fired, and I got it in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You currently work for a company called RIS Busovaca, a trucking business owned by your brother.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In 1990, sir, I believe that you became a member of the SDS, the Serbian Democratic Party, which is the main Serbian political party in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Are you still a member of that party?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe that in the first free elections held in the country you stood as a candidate for the SDS and that you were actually elected to be a member of the Busovaca parliament, the municipal parliament.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right, sir. Let me just turn your attention to a period in the first third of May of 1992. There was a confrontation in connection with the takeover of the former JNA barracks located in Kaonik. Could you tell the Court, in your own words, what you know about that confrontation, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: What I can state is that I live near that location, this is where I reside, and one day in early May I noticed a number of people gathering near the barracks. I couldn't observe everything but there were a number of people there. Later on I learned that it had to do with the takeover of the JNA barracks, which is located there, and that there was some conflicts and misunderstandings between the two parties regarding this takeover.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The gathering of people that you've just described, were they gathered at a nightclub called the Leptir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is in front of this nightclub called Leptir. Later on I learned that these were TO people from Zenica, that they came from Zenica to take over these barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, Leptir is owned by a Muslim resident of Busovaca municipality, or was at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, the owner was a Muslim. He lived in the neighbouring village of Skradno; that's where the owner is from. But the owner was a Muslim, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: These TO soldiers from Zenica, do you know whether they arrived with or without prior advance notice to the Croats, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: They came unannounced. There was no announcement of their arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Do you know anything about any agreement for arms division reached between the Croats and the Muslims in Busovaca municipality or not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: I didn't know anything about that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. What happened later in the night, as far as you're aware, Mr. Bilic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Later we learned that there were some wounded people, that there was a conflict, that there was a quarrel and that what followed was that the government in Busovaca was replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, could you tell the Court, sir, what impact that change in the municipal government had upon you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: As a citizen of that municipality, and because I do not live in the town itself but rather three kilometres outside of town, I noticed no changes. But we knew that the war was raging all around us and we were just looking to prepare food supplies. We didn't notice anything except that there were more soldiers around town.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Did you have occasion to go into town at all, into the town of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I could but I did not go to the town very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: When you did, though, did you notice that anything had changed in particular, or did it still look the same to you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: There were no particular changes which one could observe. Everything looked normal, as that was possible in circumstances like those.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You said that your objective was to prepare food supplies. Could you just elaborate a little bit upon that for the Court, Mr. Bilic. Tell the Court why that was an important goal, if it was, and what you were doing in that connection.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: It was important because there were food shortages already in town and we needed to have enough, and the refugees of Serbian ethnic background started leaving Central Bosnia and they were crossing through the Busovaca municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. We'll get to that in just a second, Mr. Bilic, but let me just ask you one question in connection with the HVO police force that replaced the old police force in Busovaca. Did you notice anything in particular in regard to the makeup of police officers?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: We couldn't notice anything because the people who were there before, who were of Serbian ethnic background, in the police, stayed in their posts. They weren't replaced so we couldn't observe anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right, sir. Did you or any of your neighbours, as far as you knew, hear anything about the municipal HVO government expelling or firing Muslims from positions of authority that they had held in the government?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: No, I haven't heard anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You just touched upon, Mr. Bilic, the subject of the passage of Serb people from Bosnia-Herzegovina, from the municipality of Zenica, through the municipality of Busovaca. Could you tell the Court when this exodus occurred and, if you know, why it occurred.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: As early as May 1992, the Serbian civilians from Zavidovici, Zepce, Breza, Visoko, Zenica municipalities started arriving in Busovaca. They had been beaten, mistreated, and abused. We had the charity organisation Dobrotvor, and this is where the refugees started coming. They were then transferred to the Serbian territory through Kiseljak. With the help of the HVO, convoys were prepared. They were leaving Busovaca to Kiseljak, and then on to the Serbian-controlled area in Radovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. In your statement, sir, you make reference to people who came from, or who were expelled from, two villages; one called Janjski Vrh and the other one called Drivusa. Did people from these two villages transit through the municipality of Busovaca, and if so, did the Croat population do anything to help them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Janjski and Drivusa were in the Zenica municipality. They were expelled from there and they came through Busovaca. We received them, fed them, and then sent them off. But it wasn't just those two villages. There were many other villages. About 30.000 ethnic Serbs came through Busovaca municipality. We provided food and shelter for them. And it wasn't that they were just transiting for one day. Some of them stayed as long as 21 days. But the HVO and local government in Busovaca provided assistance. Those people from Janjski Vrh asked assistance from their neighbours, Croat neighbours, and they helped them cross over to the Busovaca municipality, where we received them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Just one matter of historical interest. You've described an incident that occurred in the village?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: The incident which took place was in the Busovaca municipality, and the village was called Grablje. Serbs and Muslims lived together there, but it was majority Muslim. There were 13 Orthodox households. Then they were attacked, their weapons were taken from them. The people then asked for assistance from the Busovaca police. They arrived there to try to calm things down, but then a Muslim pulled out a grenade, which he then dropped, and the grenade killed him and wounded another Muslim. Then we had the meeting of the leadership of the three parties: HDZ, SDS and SDA. Mr. Kordic was also present there, and it was asked that this conflict be resolved in a peaceful way to lower the tensions and to allow people to live there in peace. He --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, you said it was asked that the conflict be resolved in a peaceful way. Who was it that made that request?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: This request was made by Mr. Kordic when we arrived in the crisis staff, that is, to find a peaceful solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And were you a participant in those discussions, Mr. Bilic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was present at this meeting and I took part in a discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So you heard Mr. Kordic's words with your own ears, so to speak, rather than filtered through someone else's recollection?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: No. I was present there in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you've already said, sir, that during 1992, about 30.000 people of Serb ethnicity left Central Bosnia, travelling through Busovaca municipality to reach Serb-held territory to the south-east of Kiseljak. A contention has been made by the Prosecution in this case that transit charges or fees were charged by the HVO in Busovaca or by Mr. Kordic to Serbs passing through the territory of Busovaca. Is there any truth to that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: There is no truth in that statement. There were no fees, there were no charges.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did the HVO and Mr. Kordic try to obstruct the passage of Serb refugees through the territory, or not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: No, they did not try to obstruct the passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Was any assistance given by the municipal HVO authorities in Busovaca municipality to the unfortunate people who had been expelled from their homes to the north, in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Yes. They provided shelter, they provided food. They even -- the Busovaca Croats even received ethnic Serbs in their homes to stay with them until they were able to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, about how many Serbs lived in Busovaca municipality before the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: About 800 ethnic Serbs lived in Busovaca municipality, and at the end of the war only about 200 remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: How many of those 200 remained in the areas that were controlled by the Muslim forces, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: The majority of ethnic Serbs lived in the villages which -- near or -- near Muslim villages or were shared with the Muslim population. None of them remained. The only Serbs who have remained in the area are in the areas controlled by the HVO. There was Grablje, Podjele, Kuber, Topala, Katici. Those villages have been completely emptied of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. As a resident of the municipality, sir, do you recall an incident that occurred at a checkpoint that was erected by the TO or the ABiH in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: An incident in summer of 1992? I don't know much about it, but I know that we were passing through that area. We had to take that road and we had to pass that checkpoint where the first incident occurred, during which two Croats were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And when were those Croats killed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Those Croats were killed -- the incident was on the 24th of January, 1993. Was it 1993? Yes, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you recall where those Croats were killed, Mr. Bilic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: That place is called Kacuni. It is also part of the Busovaca municipality, but it is some distance away from the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Could you tell us, please, whether Serbs like you, who lived in predominantly Croat-populated areas of Busovaca municipality, felt any pressure to leave their houses? Were they subjected to any pressure to do that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: We were under no pressure to leave our homes. In fact, they were telling us not to leave; to stay, to live together with them. We never had any pressure to leave. We were not under pressure to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And did the Serbs who actually stayed in the municipality end up in the Croat Muslim civil war taking sides, either Croat or Muslim? Could you tell us a little about that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: I can. We, through the Serbian Democratic Party, where we were active, we asked to stay neutral, because we were a minority population. We asked not to have to side with either the HVO or the SDA, but we said that we would defend Busovaca if this situation deteriorated. And unfortunately, the situation did deteriorate and we had to join with the HDZ to defend Busovaca from the Muslim attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just one question along the lines of what you've just said, Mr. Bilic. Was there any pressure or compulsion exerted upon you or your fellow Serbs to join the HVO and to link arms with Croats against the Muslims, or not? Tell us about that, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: There was no coercion on the part of the local government at the time. It was all based on agreement and what Mr. Kordic said. He would -- he didn't want to have Serbs go to the front lines, where there were front lines against the Serbs. He said that it wasn't right for the ethnic Serbs to fight, the ethnic Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just one more question concerning the time before the war broke out in Busovaca in January of 1993. Can you think of any incidents of mistreatment of Serbs by Muslims in the Lasva Valley? And if you can, could you just tell us a little about that, Mr. Bilic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can recall that on the 13th of June, 1993, the village of Grablje was attacked, those 13 homes, populated by Serbs, and they took the weapons away from them. And this is when we asked local Busovaca police to come and protect us, and they came and protected us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were there any incidents in which a Serbian priest had been mistreated and anything that you were asked to do in that regard, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Florijan Glavocevic asked me to go to Travnik, because a Serb priest had been harassed in Novi Travnik, to get him out and bring him to Busovaca. One of HVO Croats, or rather he was with the police, he worked for the police, and he went with me. We brought that priest to Busovaca and then on to the Serb side. And also, as for the town of Busovaca, in 1991, before the war, the flat of the priest who lived in Busovaca was robbed. In 1992 his flat was robbed twice. We found the jacket of the young man who had perpetrated this offence, and he was of Muslim origin. Subsequently we found out that he was selling the priest's property in Livno and other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just addressing your attention to the outbreak of the war, sir, who attacked whom?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Muslims in that part of our land, the Muslims attacked the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And if I might just take you through this fairly quickly, Mr. Bilic. I believe that you were called upon by the HVO to dig trenches for your mutual defence against the ABiH on January the 24th, 1993, in the village of Skradno.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Well, trenches were not dug before that. On the 24th of January, 1994 [as interpreted], I was asked to go dig trenches in the village of Skradno. That is the day of the incident. That is the day when two Croats were killed in Kacuni. And after that I no longer went to dig trenches, and instead I assumed the duties of the priest in the town of Busovaca, and they did not ask me to go dig trenches or do similar chores again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. How about in April of 1993? Were you called upon to report to the HVO for work duty?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: I was not called to report to work duty before. It was the first time, on the 24th of April, 1993. 1992 nobody asked me to do that, because I had other duties. For a while I worked in Dobrotvor and was organising the passage of Serb refugees through the town of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't propose to ask any questions about paragraph 17. The Prosecution can cross-examine on that if they wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, going on to paragraph 18 of your outline, for the Court's information, Mr. Bilic, we've heard a lot of evidence about Croats leaving ABiH-controlled parts of the municipality of Busovaca to the south. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Most -- half of the Croats in the municipality of Busovaca left. They had trouble there, because Muslims were attacking them since they were a majority population in that area, and those Croats left the town because they had been attacked. And it became particularly difficult when in June 1993 refugees arrived from all sides, from Guca Gora and from the Travnik municipality. And then the demographic structure of the population changed so that the number of incidents grew and there was less order in our life. And then the incidents escalated in November 1993, when the Serbs took the town of Jajce, and all of the Croat refugees were then expelled and moved towards Travnik and Busovaca. Many of those refugees came straight to Busovaca. And this resulted in lawlessness and impossibility to control everybody's behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, you said that the Serbs took the town of Jajce -- you mean the Bosnian Serb army or BSA -- in November of 1993. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The first refugees arrived on the 1st of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Are you sure about the year there, sir? Is it 1993 or should it you be 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm sorry. It was 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, we've heard a lot of evidence about Muslims moving out of the town of Busovaca with their families. Were there any Muslim families that stayed, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Yes. Some Muslims stayed in Busovaca. Their families lived as we did. I mean, I don't know if you can call it normal life under wartime conditions. But food was provided for the Serbs and Croats and Muslims, because food was being distributed from one centre. So we were provided. And those who stayed behind suffered no consequences, nor were they harassed. Those who had jobs continued to go to those jobs. They were not fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. We've also heard evidence in this case about the problems caused by snipers and artillery, specifically Muslim snipers and ABiH artillery. Do you have any experience or observations to add with respect to the frequency of sniping incidents or shelling of the town of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Well, Busovaca was shelled almost every day. Until 1993, I can merely confirm that we could not have any funerals by day, we always had to bury people at night, because even cemeteries, the whole of the town, places around the town, were all shelled by day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, you've described the influx of refugees and the problems that that caused, involving the increase in incidents, as you put it; I might suggest to you "the crime rate" might be a way to view that. Could you tell the Court whether any particular group was targeted by this crime wave, or were all three ethnic groups, or principal ethnic groups, victims of this criminal activity?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: All three ethnicities were victimised by such activities. I didn't see any one in particular have initiative or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right, sir. Is it the case that throughout the war the civilian community relied for sustenance principally upon the delivery of supplies of humanitarian aid to the municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Was there any discrimination in the allocation of humanitarian aid supplies to one particular or a number of particular ethnic groups as opposed to another?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: No. Food was equally distributed among all the ethnic groups in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you, sir, were one of the heads of Dobrotvor, or you were the head of Dobrotvor, the Serb humanitarian organisation in Busovaca, I believe.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever make deliveries of food received by you on behalf of Dobrotvor to Muslims that lived in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Yes. Muslims shared the list with us, and they received food relief at the same time that we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right, sir. Now, one of the principal claims being made by the Prosecution in this case is that Bosnian Croat political organisations, including the HDZ-BiH, engaged in a campaign of discrimination or persecution, or adopted a policy of persecution and harassment specifically of Bosnian Muslim civilians throughout the Lasva Valley, but also specifically in Busovaca. Could you give the Court your perception, as a resident of the municipality, sir, throughout those difficult years, whether there's any force or substance in that version of events.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: In my view, and I lived there, there were no pressures at all, nor any attempts made to have some population evicted from that territory, at least that is not something that I ever noticed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you yourself obviously are not a Croat, but have you ever been involved in any Bosnian Croat political organisations?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: As a private citizen, sir, have you ever heard discussions amongst your Croat colleagues --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: When did you first meet Mr. Kordic, Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: In 1992. I met him in the municipal hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Did Mr. Kordic express any views in regard to whether Serb residents of the municipality should stay or go?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic always said that we should not leave, that we should remain, in our hearts, and also told us to prevail upon our other Serbs who wanted to go, and saying that, "If one of you goes, then the whole village will leave." He was one of the first people who were trying to prevail upon us not to leave our hearts in that town.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did he attempt in any way to give help to the Serb community, the Serb residents in the municipality of Busovaca, throughout the war, as far as you could see?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: We were full-fledged citizens there, enjoying equitable treatment. When food was distributed or perhaps fuel for agricultural machinery, or anything else, we shared it all with Croats and with Muslims on an equitable footing. There was no discrimination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The Court's heard considerable evidence about Mr. Kordic's public speaking activities. Have you ever heard Mr. Kordic refer to anyone, any group, any person, in a derogatory manner, or make any attempt to incite violence against any ethnic group, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: From all the times I talked with Mr. Kordic or listened to him talking, I never heard him say anything like that or use derogatory terms against anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: How would you characterise, from your personal perspective, Mr. Kordic's attitude towards the various ethnic groups that lived in the municipality, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: As I see it, he has a positive attitude towards all the communities which lived in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There was one point, I believe, sir, in 1992 when you asked the Central Bosnia Operative Zone commander of the HVO, Colonel Blaskic, to help you organise a convoy of Serbs that were leaving from Zenica. Could you just tell the Court what the response to that inquiry was.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: As a paper had to be signed for the passage of the convoy, I had to go and talk to Colonel Blaskic to ask him for permission to pass through Busovaca. He replied, "I have nothing to do with that matter because that is a civilian matter. Talk to Mr. Kordic." And then I went to Mr. Kordic and was issued the pass for the convoy which was to go through Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, indeed, Mr. Bilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. No, sir. Thank you. I don't have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Bilic, how long has your family been in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: My family has lived in that part of Busovaca for over 200 years.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are both your parents Serb?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Is your spouse Serb?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: She is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you have adult children, and if so, are any of them married to a --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: -- are any of them married to a non-Serb?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would you name the child, and would you name the non-Serb group to which that child is married?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: There are about 30 per cent mixed marriages in my family. My two brothers are married to Croats. I have a nephew. We have a very mixed family.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your children, are they married to Croats or Serbs or any other ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: A daughter of mine is married to a man whose father is a Croat and whose mother is a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are these children living in Busovaca? I could not tell from the summary if they are living physically with you or simply in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: No, she does not live in Busovaca any more. She married in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was her husband at any time a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: I don't know. He used to live in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were any of your relatives ever members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Which degree of kinship?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: -- but that was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Which relatives? How close were they to you, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: My two brothers were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where were they living? Which municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: The municipality of Busovaca is where they lived, and where they still live.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I mean no offence by the term that I'm going to use but I need to ask you your reaction to it. The term "Chetnik," when used about Serbs, do you consider that an offensive term? If someone called you a Chetnik, would you be offended?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you if perhaps you may have heard -- and I would ask the Chamber and counsel opposing just to refer to Z173, it was a press conference given by Dario Kordic, on 28 July 1992 -- I just wondered, if I may read this to you briefly, there is just a sentence that I would ask your reaction to. Mr. Kordic is asked a question and his response is: "All right. You asked three questions. I will not take long. The gentleman, primarily Mr. Ignac, will add whatever is necessary. Mr. Tiho will give you his assessment of the situation on the front line and whether anything can change. The information we have is that a large-scale regrouping of Chetniks --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: "The information that we have is that a large-scale grouping of Chetnik forces is taking place. From it we deduce that this grouping does not have a picnic or weekend in mind but probably new combat operations." I will stop there. Had you heard, perhaps in listening to the radio or watching television, this particular comment made by Dario Kordic, referring to the Serb troops as Chetnik forces?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Because you were involved in the political work of the SDS party, I'd like to ask a few questions, if I may. In 1990, exactly what was your role in the Busovaca municipal parliament? Did you serve on any particularly important committees or have any particularly important functions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: I was a councilman.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How many members of the SDS party were serving in the Busovaca municipal parliament?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: They were elected on the basis of the population structure. So according to the number of votes that each of the groups received, that determined the number of seats.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: While you served, how many were serving, how many Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: There were three of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Could you be kind enough to name them.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Milorad Jovic, Bozidar Hercegovac, and myself, Zoran Bilic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When did you leave the SDS, and for what reason?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Well, when, what you call it, the war started, when war broke out and Jajce was taken, Busovaca was cut off. We simply could not communicate with other people and we simply were left there. We could not communicate with the rest of the party and that was that. But we decided not to join any other party. I was the only member of the SDS. The other two Serbs, they were not members of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I must ask you, please, to be specific about the dates when you left the SDS, and when you, in fact, left your life as a political figure in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: It was in early 1992 that I stopped being actively involved in politics.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you please give me a month in 1992 when you stopped being active in politics.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Well, I was never really an active politician, I was merely a municipal councilman, which was not politics, as one understands it. It had to do with the life and work and the operation of the municipality, nothing but the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When did you step down from the assembly or the parliament?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: When my term expired. We were regularly elected, and when my term expired, I quit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Which was what month; what year?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the month or the year.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you follow carefully the developments of your one-time party as they unfolded in Sarajevo and Pale? Specifically, let's say, between 1991 and 1992, did you follow those developments?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: I could not and I did not because the media were disrupted, and there was no other way to come by any information.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Which media were disrupted?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Radio and television. We simply could not watch, that is, listen to any.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that during the years 1991 and 1992 you had no access to either radio or television?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I had no access to the channels which were informing -- which were covering other sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So you were completely in the dark about the nationalism which was overtaking the platform of the SDS in 1991/1992. Did you not follow Karadzic's pushing of the party into a certain direction?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you ever in the military?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Who is Jovan Divjak?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was an officer in the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Afterward did he remain in the Yugoslav People's Army or did he go to another army?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know who Stjepan Siber was, and what nationality?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was Divjak a Serb?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Again, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How do you feel about Serbs and Croats who remained -- forget the Croat part. Excuse me. How do you feel about Serbs who remained in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and didn't go into, let's say, the HVO or the army of the Serb Republic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: That was their option, their choice, their view, their option. I have nothing to say about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you personally, prior to the time you call the conflict -- and I'm not exactly clear when you see the conflict starting -- but did you personally ever have a very bad experience with a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Me, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Why did you take the position that you would go with the HVO as opposed to the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Because in those early days, when parties were being created, then at that time the SDA and HDZ appeared to be in a coalition.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And when was that? Can you please give us a month and a year?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: I couldn't give you dates, but that was 1991, right after the elections.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: But in 1992 -- I just want to make sure I understood your evidence correctly -- you indicated that if Busovaca were attacked, you would fight for it. Why did you fight the ABiH as opposed to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: We said that we will fight the one who attacked Busovaca, and would not join any party or any options, either the HDZ or the SDA. And had the HDZ attacked Busovaca, we would have stayed with the Muslims, but because it was Muslims who attacked Busovaca, we stayed there to defend the places where they lived.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would like to ask you if you can give me an actual date and place of the attacks by the Muslim -- or by the ABiH in Busovaca. Please be very specific.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: I was not in the army, but I know that on the 24th of January, 1993, we -- they told us that we should turn back and go home because two Croats had been killed at Kacuni. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Who told you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: A messenger came, some kind of a messenger. We were digging trenches at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: A messenger from an army, bearing a uniform? What kind of messenger?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: They sent someone that the Kacuni Croats were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but who sent someone? I need to know who sent this messenger, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And did you believe a messenger, whom you did not know, from a source you did not know? Did you act on his words?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: This messenger didn't tell us. He told us the man who had brought us to dig trenches. Then this man told us, "Stop digging. Go home. There was an incident."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you living in the Busovaca area on the 20th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: I don't live in the town itself; I live in a village about three kilometres out of town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What is the name of that little hamlet that you described?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Granice, in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you there on the 20th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And how far, in kilometres, can you tell us that town is from the town of Busovaca, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: The village of Granice is about three, three and a half kilometres from Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you not hear explosion after explosion after explosion on the night of the 20th of January, 1993 from your little hamlet three kilometres from Busovaca town?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: You couldn't hear, because the hamlet is tucked away. I did not hear it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you see smoke the next morning from business after business after business having been blown up?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: I did not observe anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you hear any rumours in town that such a thing had occurred?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, subsequently. I heard about it later, because I didn't go to town very much, but later on I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How often did you go to town, and why did you go to town?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: I did not go to town very often. I went there when they were distributing food. That's when I went there. And sometimes I would go there to open up the church. The church was in the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where was the distribution centre for the food in the town? Location, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Near the Serbian church there was -- that is where Dobrotvor organisation had its headquarters, and the central warehouse was in the central part of town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And is the Serbian church still standing today?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: During what period of time, from when to when, did you work with Dobrotvor?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: The organisation was established in early 1982 [as interpreted] and it worked until 1994. Then it stopped working, because from then on all the food was distributed from one central location.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The transcript says "from early 1982." Dobrotvor was working from early 1982? Is that a correct year?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: You said which year?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: My question to you is: When did you work from -- during what period did you work in Dobrotvor?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: I was mentioning 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So you worked from 1992 until 1994, the whole time it was open; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you restrict your work to the municipality of Busovaca, or did you physically work in Zenica as well?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: Only in the territory of Busovaca municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you work with UNHCR personnel?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN BILIC
utterances.text: They came occasionally to ask us how we were. We did not cooperate with them. I don't know what they were called. The European Union something. But they would only come occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You made -- I will want to discuss the -- working backward a little bit, deliberately, I want to discuss with you some of the points of the incidents in May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask the Court -- 10 after would be our deadline -- would it be better if I just commenced tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, probably more convenient. Mr. Bilic, we're going to adjourn now for the day, and if you would be back --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- to conclude your evidence. Could you remember during the adjournment not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that includes members of the Defence team. Could you be back, please, at half past 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.
